# The Architecture of Unremembered Time

## Prologue: The First Map

There is an old cartographic manuscript, preserved in the vault of a quiet university library whose name is best left unspoken, drawn upon vellum so thin it seems woven from pressed light. It depicts no continent known to modern geography. Its coastlines do not conform to the drift of South America or the jagged fjords of Scandinavia, nor does it portray the mythical, symmetrical balance of the ancient Greek *oikoumene*. Instead, it depicts a single, vast archipelago shaped like a shattered hourglass, surrounded by an ocean labeled simply: *Mare Incognitum et Silex*—The Unknown and Flinty Sea.

What makes this map peculiar is not its phantom topography, but its legend. In place of standard notations for anchorages, shoals, or trade winds, the anonymous cartographer wrote directions based entirely on human states of attention. *Here, the sea grows thick with forgotten names.* *Here, the current moves only when unobserved.* *Here, the islander’s voice becomes the wind before it reaches the shore.*

For centuries, mapmakers were concerned not merely with where things were, but with what things meant. Geography was an extension of cosmology, and cosmology was an attempt to build a bridge between the small, flickering candle of human consciousness and the vast, cold dark of the universe. To draw a map was to perform an act of resistance against oblivion. It was an assertion that a place, once named, could not entirely vanish.

Yet places do vanish. Entire empires—their languages, their distinct smells of scorched pine and boiled vinegar, their specific lullabies and tax codes—collapse into layers of compressed dark soil no thicker than a fingernail. We walk every day across the unread library of the earth. Underneath the asphalt of modern cities lie the bones of forgotten forests, the ashes of hearths lit by hands whose genetic lines ended ten thousand years ago, and the quiet, petrified echoes of words that had no translation.

This is an essay, a meditation, and a narrative excursion into that hidden territory: the architecture of unremembered time, the ways we construct meaning in the face of impermanence, and the quiet art of charting the invisible.

---

## I. The Paleontology of Thought

Consider the stone. Not as an obstacle or a building material, but as an archive.

In the limestone quarries of the Jura Mountains, one can find the calcified remains of ancient ammonites—mollusks that swam through warm, shallow seas during the Jurassic period. Their shells form perfect logarithmic spirals, mathematical beauty preserved in gray rock. When you hold one of these fossils, your thumb rests in a groove that was smoothed by the movement of water a hundred and fifty million years ago.

Between that ancient sea and your hand lies a expanse of time so vast that the human mind flinches from it. We are evolutionarily ill-equipped to comprehend deep time. Our ancestors needed to understand the duration of a season, the life cycle of a deer, the time it took for a child to grow old enough to gather berries or hold a spear. Our internal clocks are tuned to the rising and setting of a local star, calibrated in heartbeats and breath cycles.

When we are confronted with geological time—with millions and billions of years—our sense of scale collapses. We reduce it to abstract numbers, but numbers carry no weight in the gut. To feel deep time, one must look at the way a river cuts through granite, or how the steps of an ancient amphitheater in Anatolia have been hollowed out by the soft, cumulative friction of millions of leather-soled shoes.

Thought, too, has a paleontology.

The concepts we inhabit today are built upon the fossilized remains of dead metaphors. When we speak of "deliberation," we are invoking the Latin *libra*, the balance scale; we are mentally weighing lead weights in an ancient market. When we say someone is "sincere," we may be reaching back—if the popular, dubious etymology is to be believed—to the Roman stonecutters who used *sine cera* (without wax) to assure buyers that a marble statue had no hidden cracks filled with tinted paraffin. Every word in our mouths is a ruin that has been rebuilt, renovated, and inhabited by successive generations of tenants who have long since forgotten who laid the original foundation.

Language is the sediment of human experience. Just as the geologist reads the history of the earth in layers of basalt, sandstone, and shale, the philologist reads the history of human feeling in the shifts of vowels and the decay of consonants.

In the early centuries of the common era, the Gothic language was spoken across vast swathes of Europe. It was the language of Ulfilas, who translated the Bible using an alphabet he invented specifically for the task. Today, Gothic is dead. No child learns it at a mother’s knee; no lover whispers it in the dark. It exists only in fragment manuscript folios, its grammar reconstructed by patient scholars working in quiet rooms. A whole way of perceiving the world—the specific nuances of how a Gothic speaker perceived the glint of frost on an oak leaf, or the precise emotional weight they gave to grief or courage—has evaporated into the air.

Where do dead languages go? They do not float in the ether like displaced ghosts. They simply dissolve into the background noise of the cosmos, joining the soft, background radiation left over from the Big Bang. They become part of the dark matter of history: unobserved, unmeasured, but exerting a gravitational pull on everything that followed.

---

## II. The Archives of Sunder

Let us imagine a place.

In the high, dry tablelands of a forgotten province, built into the basalt cliffside of a dormant caldera, stands the city of Sunder. It is not a city of trade or war, but a city of catalogers. For seven hundred years, the Order of the Silent Chronometer has inhabited Sunder with a single, bizarre mandate: to document things that have ceased to exist without leaving a physical trace.

The scholars of Sunder do not collect pottery shards, coins, or arrowheads. They leave such material detritus to the antiquarians of the lowlands. Instead, they collect lost phenomena.

In the great subterranean vaults of Sunder, cataloged on thousands of rolls of linen paper dipped in beeswax, one can find meticulous entries for:

*   *The specific scent of the rain that fell on the island of Crete on the afternoon of May 14th, 1342 BCE.*
*   *The melody played by an unnamed shepherd boy on a reed pipe near the ruins of Persepolis, heard by no one except a stray hound, in the winter of 630 CE.*
*   *The exact shape of the shadow cast by a dying olive tree onto a whitewashed wall in a village that was swept away by a mudslide three minutes later.*

If you were to ask the Master of the Archive how such things can be known, he would look at you with eyes faded by decades of candle smoke and answer: *"Nothing is lost; it is merely dispersed."*

The philosophy of Sunder rests on a single physical intuition: the universe is a closed system. Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transformed. When a sound is uttered, the kinetic energy of that vibration moves through the air molecules, striking walls, leaves, skin, and soil. The wave dampens, spreads, and weakens, but its motion does not vanish into absolute zero; it is converted into microscopic thermal currents, infinitesimally warming the surfaces it encounters.

In theory, if one possessed an instrument of infinite sensitivity, one could read the thermal pattern of a stone wall and reconstruct every word ever spoken in its presence. The wall is a phonograph record; the air has been the stylus; time is the arm that sweeps across the groove.

The scribes of Sunder spend their lives building mental instruments of that infinite sensitivity. They sit in absolute silence in stone cells carved from the volcanic rock, listening not to the present air, but to the deep thermal noise of the world. They track the faint ripples of forgotten events as they echo down through the physical substratum of reality.

Is Sunder real?

Of course not. It is a myth, an allegory, a literary ghost invented to give form to a longing that every conscious human feels at some point in their life: the longing for a witness.

We live our lives in a state of profound privacy. Even our closest companions know only a fraction of our inner landscape. They do not see the thousands of split-second thoughts that flash through our minds as we watch a shadow creep across a rug, or the sudden, unprovoked pangs of nostalgia brought on by the smell of ozone before a summer thunderstorm. Most of human experience takes place in complete solitude, unrecorded, unshared, and unremembered.

We build monuments, write books, plant trees, and record videos in a desperate attempt to post sentinels along the perimeter of our lives. We say to the future: *Look, I was here. I felt this. I saw that light.*

But time is an unyielding tide. It wears away the granite inscription; it rots the magnetic tape; it scrambles the digital bits stored in server farms beneath the desert. Eventually, even the memory of our species will fade, and the Earth will continue to spin—a blue and white marble drifting through the dark—bearing no sign that it once harbored creatures who wept over poetry and spent centuries trying to measure the distance to the stars.

---

## III. The Cartography of Silence

If physical permanence is an illusion, what remains?

Perhaps the answer lies in shifting our perspective from the duration of a thing to its quality. We are obsessed with survival, with making things last. But longevity is not the only metric of value. A flower that blooms for a single night—such as the *Epiphyllum oxypetalum*, the Night-blooming Cereus—is no less real or beautiful than a mountain that stands for fifty million years. Indeed, its very transience gives its beauty an edge, a sharpness that the mountain lacks.

In traditional Japanese aesthetics, this concept is captured by the phrase *mono no aware*—a deep, gentle sadness at the impermanence of things, coupled with a profound appreciation for their fleeting reality. It is the emotion felt when watching cherry blossoms fall, knowing that their display will last only a few days before the rain sweeps the petals into the mud. The sadness and the beauty are not separate; they are two sides of the same coin. The blossom is beautiful *because* it falls.

Consider the nature of silence.

We tend to think of silence as an absence—a void, a lack of sound. But any sound engineer will tell you that there is no such thing as absolute silence in the natural world. Even in an anechoic chamber, a room designed to absorb all sound reflections, a human being will soon begin to hear two distinct noises: a high-pitched whine and a low, thumping roar. The high sound is the operation of the nervous system; the low sound is the circulation of blood through the ears.

Silence is not emptiness; it is a context. It is the canvas upon which sound is painted. Without silence, music would be nothing more than an unbearable wall of static noise. Without the spaces between words, language would collapse into a meaningless, continuous roar.

In geography, the blank spaces on the map—the *terra incognita*—were long viewed as failures of knowledge, blank canvas waiting to be filled with gridlines, names, and administrative boundaries. But to early explorers and dreamers, those blank spaces were the most vital parts of the map. They were the spaces where possibility lived, where the imagination could construct impossible cities, strange beasts, and utopian societies.

When we cartograph every square meter of the Earth with high-resolution satellite imagery, when every alleyway can be traversed virtually via a smartphone screen, we eliminate the blank spaces. We achieve total legibility, but in doing so, we lose a specific kind of wonder. We flatten the world into a vast, searchable database.

Yet, true *terra incognita* has not vanished; it has merely migrated. It has moved inward, into the unmapped wilderness of the human interior, and outward, into the unfathomable depths of the cosmic ocean.

---

## IV. The Geometry of Starlight

Look up at the night sky on a clear winter midnight, away from the glare of streetlights and neon signs.

The light that strikes your retina from the star Betelgeuse, hanging red and heavy in the shoulder of Orion, left its source roughly six hundred years ago. It began its journey across the vacuum of space during the Late Middle Ages. When those photons were emitted, the printing press had not yet been invented in Europe, the Western Hemisphere was entirely unknown to Old World cartographers, and the Black Death was still a fresh, terrifying memory in the cities of the Mediterranean.

For six centuries, those light packets traveled at 186,000 miles per second through absolute cold and silence, crossing trillions of miles of empty space, unobserved, untouched, uninterrupted. And then, in a fraction of a microsecond, they pass through your cornea, focus through your lens, and strike the rods and cones at the back of your eye, triggering a tiny electrical impulse that your brain interprets as a faint, reddish point of light.

In that moment, a direct connection is established between a distant, dying red supergiant star and a conscious human mind. You are not merely looking at the star; you are intersecting with its history. You are looking back in time.

The night sky is a temporal collage. The light from Sirius is eight years old; the light from Vega is twenty-five years old; the light from the Andromeda Galaxy—a faint, misty smudge visible to the naked eye under dark skies—left its source two and a half million years ago. When that light began its journey across the intergalactic void, our ancestors were small, bipedal hominins roaming the African savanna, who had not yet mastered the art of making stone axes, let alone looking at the sky and wondering what the stars were.

To look up at night is to look into a museum of ancient light. It is an architecture of time made visible through photon streams.

And yet, this vast display is largely silent. The stars do not broadcast their histories in human words. They speak in the language of physics: spectral lines, Doppler shifts, gravitational waves, and thermal radiation. They tell us what they are made of, how fast they are moving, and how they will eventually die, but they tell us nothing about what it means to observe them.

The meaning is something we bring to the dark. We are the cosmos waking up and looking at itself in the mirror.

As the astronomer Carl Sagan famously observed, we are made of "star-stuff." The carbon in our DNA, the iron in our hemoglobin, the calcium in our teeth, and the silicon in our computer chips were all forged in the nuclear furnaces of ancient stars that exploded billions of years ago. We are recycled starlight, organized for a brief, fragile moment into complex biological structures capable of feeling joy, sorrow, curiosity, and awe.

When we consider our existence from this perspective, the terror of impermanence shifts into something closer to gratitude. We are not separate from the universe, struggling against its cold indifference; we *are* the universe, experiencing a temporary moment of self-awareness.

---

## V. The Threshold of the Forest

Let us return to the earth, to a smaller, more intimate scale.

In the Pacific Northwest of North America, there are old-growth temperate rainforests where Douglas firs and Western red cedars have stood for nearly a thousand years. The forest floor is soft and spongy, carpeted with thick layers of moss, ferns, and decaying wood.

When a giant tree finally falls—struck by lightning, undermined by a winter storm, or simply overcome by the slow weight of centuries—it does not disappear. It becomes what ecologists call a "nurse log."

As the fallen giant slowly decomposes over centuries, it provides a moisture-rich, nutrient-dense nursery for new seeds. Rows of young hemlocks and firs take root along the back of the dead trunk, their roots reaching down around its mossy sides to penetrate the soil below. Decades later, long after the original log has fully rotted away into black humus, you can see lines of mature trees standing in a straight, unnatural row, suspended on high, stilt-like roots that outline the ghost of the fallen elder that fed them.

This is the logic of the forest: life built directly upon the architecture of decay. Nothing is wasted. Death is not an interruption of the system, but its fundamental engine.

Human culture operates on the same ecological principle, though we are often reluctant to admit it.

We build our philosophies, our art, and our political systems upon the nurse logs of dead civilizations. The Renaissance was born from the rediscovered corpses of Greek and Roman manuscripts that had spent centuries gathering dust in monastery libraries and Islamic scholars' studies. Modern science grew out of the fertile decay of medieval alchemy and natural philosophy. Our fairy tales are the eroded husks of ancient religious myths, stripped of their terrifying liturgical weight and converted into bedtime stories for children.

We live in a landscape of cultural nurse logs. We draw sustenance from the dead, and one day, our own ideas, institutions, and creative works will become the soft, dark soil from which future generations draw their nourishment.

There is a quiet comfort in this continuity. It frees us from the impossible burden of having to build something that lasts forever. We do not need to construct eternal pyramids; we need only to be good soil.

---

## VI. The Art of the Unmapped Present

In the modern world, we are tormented by a hyper-awareness of time.

We live by the calendar and the clock, divided into micro-intervals of productivity, notifications, deadlines, and schedules. We archive our lives in real-time, uploading photos of our meals, our walks, our thoughts, and our faces to digital networks that promise to keep them safe in "the cloud"—a delightfully poetic euphemism for thousands of humming, energy-hungry server racks housed in concrete warehouses scattered across the globe.

We are terrified of being forgotten, yet we spend very little time actually inhabiting the present moment. We are constantly capturing the moment for *later*, turning our experiences into souvenirs before they have even fully unfolded.

We walk through a museum and look at the paintings through the lens of a smartphone screen, ensuring we have a digital record of the art while ignoring the physical canvas hanging three feet in front of us. We attend concerts and view the performance through a sea of glowing rectangles, prioritizing the proof of attendance over the immediate, visceral experience of sound moving through the air.

In doing so, we turn ourselves into cartographers who are so obsessed with drawing the map that we never actually step foot on the land.

What would it mean to live without the constant urge to record and preserve? What would it mean to cultivate an appreciation for the unmapped present?

It would mean accepting that some experiences are valuable *precisely because* they are private, transient, and unrepeatable.

Think of a conversation with an old friend on a late night in early autumn. You are sitting on a porch, wrapped in blankets, drinking tea or wine. The air is crisp, smelling of woodsmoke and damp leaves. You talk about everything and nothing—old memories, quiet fears, absurd jokes that would make no sense to anyone else. There is no recording device running. No one posts an update about it. It leaves no trace on the digital ether.

When the night ends and you go to sleep, that conversation exists only in two minds. As the years pass, those memories will fade, shift, and eventually disappear entirely.

Was that conversation any less real, any less meaningful, because it was not preserved for posterity?

No. If anything, its ephemerality gives it a sacred quality. It was a secret shared between two people and the night air—a temporary gathering of warmth and presence against the backdrop of the cold, silent universe. It was a piece of pure architecture built out of unremembered time.

---

## VII. The Unfinished Chart

Imagine returning to that library vault mentioned at the beginning of this essay, to the room where the thin, light-woven vellum map is kept.

If you look closely at the edges of that chart, past the shattered hourglass archipelago and beyond the *Mare Incognitum et Silex*, you will notice that the ink fades gradually into the blank margin. The cartographer did not draw a neat, decorative border to seal off their work. They simply stopped drawing.

The margin is not an error; it is an invitation.

It acknowledges that every map is incomplete, every history is partial, and every human attempt to measure and catalog the world will eventually reach an edge where knowledge dissolves into wonder, and memory gives way to silence.

We are all cartographers of the dark. We navigate our brief lives using incomplete charts, guided by the ancient, distant light of long-dead stars, steering our small vessels through waters that have swallowed thousands of forgotten fleets before us.

We will not leave a mark that endures forever. The waves will smooth the sand where we walked; the moss will carpet the stones we laid; the cold solar wind will eventually sweep across an empty earth.

But that is not a tragedy.

The tragedy would be to pass through this vast, mysterious, heartbreakingly beautiful world without ever having looked up at the night sky in wonder, without ever having listened to the thermal noise of an ancient wall, without ever having built a shelter of quiet warmth in the middle of the winter dark.

The value of the map is not in its permanence, but in the journey it inspires. The value of time is not in its duration, but in its intensity.

Let the archives of Sunder stay hidden in their volcanic cliffside. Let the dead languages rest quietly in their folios. Let the stars burn through their nuclear fuel in the deep galactic night.

Here, now, in this unmapped breath, on this small blue world spinning through the dark, the light is clear, the air is cold, and the blank page is open before us.

Draw the line. Write the name. Step out into the unknown coast, and begin.

And then, in a fraction of a microsecond, they pass through your cornea, focus through your lens, and strike the rods and cones at the back of your eye, triggering a tiny electrical impulse that your brain interprets as a faint, reddish point of light.

In that moment, a direct connection is established between a distant, dying red supergiant star and a conscious human mind. You are not merely looking at the star; you are intersecting with its history. You are looking back in time.

The night sky is a temporal collage. The light from Sirius is eight years old; the light from Vega is twenty-five years old; the light from the Andromeda Galaxy—a faint, misty smudge visible to the naked eye under dark skies—left its source two and a half million years ago. When that light began its journey across the intergalactic void, our ancestors were small, bipedal hominins roaming the African savanna, who had not yet mastered the art of making stone axes, let alone looking at the sky and wondering what the stars were.

To look up at night is to look into a museum of ancient light. It is an architecture of time made visible through photon streams.

And yet, this vast display is largely silent. The stars do not broadcast their histories in human words. They speak in the language of physics: spectral lines, Doppler shifts, gravitational waves, and thermal radiation. They tell us what they are made of, how fast they are moving, and how they will eventually die, but they tell us nothing about what it means to observe them.

The meaning is something we bring to the dark. We are the cosmos waking up and looking at itself in the mirror.

As the astronomer Carl Sagan famously observed, we are made of "star-stuff." The carbon in our DNA, the iron in our hemoglobin, the calcium in our teeth, and the silicon in our computer chips were all forged in the nuclear furnaces of ancient stars that exploded billions of years ago. We are recycled starlight, organized for a brief, fragile moment into complex biological structures capable of feeling joy, sorrow, curiosity, and awe.

When we consider our existence from this perspective, the terror of impermanence shifts into something closer to gratitude. We are not separate from the universe, struggling against its cold indifference; we *are* the universe, experiencing a temporary moment of self-awareness.

---

## V. The Threshold of the Forest

Let us return to the earth, to a smaller, more intimate scale.

In the Pacific Northwest of North America, there are old-growth temperate rainforests where Douglas firs and Western red cedars have stood for nearly a thousand years. The forest floor is soft and spongy, carpeted with thick layers of moss, ferns, and decaying wood.

When a giant tree finally falls—struck by lightning, undermined by a winter storm, or simply overcome by the slow weight of centuries—it does not disappear. It becomes what ecologists call a "nurse log."

As the fallen giant slowly decomposes over centuries, it provides a moisture-rich, nutrient-dense nursery for new seeds. Rows of young hemlocks and firs take root along the back of the dead trunk, their roots reaching down around its mossy sides to penetrate the soil below. Decades later, long after the original log has fully rotted away into black humus, you can see lines of mature trees standing in a straight, unnatural row, suspended on high, stilt-like roots that outline the ghost of the fallen elder that fed them.

This is the logic of the forest: life built directly upon the architecture of decay. Nothing is wasted. Death is not an interruption of the system, but its fundamental engine.

Human culture operates on the same ecological principle, though we are often reluctant to admit it.

We build our philosophies, our art, and our political systems upon the nurse logs of dead civilizations. The Renaissance was born from the rediscovered corpses of Greek and Roman manuscripts that had spent centuries gathering dust in monastery libraries and Islamic scholars' studies. Modern science grew out of the fertile decay of medieval alchemy and natural philosophy. Our fairy tales are the eroded husks of ancient religious myths, stripped of their terrifying liturgical weight and converted into bedtime stories for children.

We live in a landscape of cultural nurse logs. We draw sustenance from the dead, and one day, our own ideas, institutions, and creative works will become the soft, dark soil from which future generations draw their nourishment.

There is a quiet comfort in this continuity. It frees us from the impossible burden of having to build something that lasts forever. We do not need to construct eternal pyramids; we need only to be good soil.

---

## VI. The Art of the Unmapped Present

In the modern world, we are tormented by a hyper-awareness of time.

We live by the calendar and the clock, divided into micro-intervals of productivity, notifications, deadlines, and schedules. We archive our lives in real-time, uploading photos of our meals, our walks, our thoughts, and our faces to digital networks that promise to keep them safe in "the cloud"—a delightfully poetic euphemism for thousands of humming, energy-hungry server racks housed in concrete warehouses scattered across the globe.

We are terrified of being forgotten, yet we spend very little time actually inhabiting the present moment. We are constantly capturing the moment for *later*, turning our experiences into souvenirs before they have even fully unfolded.

We walk through a museum and look at the paintings through the lens of a smartphone screen, ensuring we have a digital record of the art while ignoring the physical canvas hanging three feet in front of us. We attend concerts and view the performance through a sea of glowing rectangles, prioritizing the proof of attendance over the immediate, visceral experience of sound moving through the air.

In doing so, we turn ourselves into cartographers who are so obsessed with drawing the map that we never actually step foot on the land.

What would it mean to live without the constant urge to record and preserve? What would it mean to cultivate an appreciation for the unmapped present?

It would mean accepting that some experiences are valuable *precisely because* they are private, transient, and unrepeatable.

Think of a conversation with an old friend on a late night in early autumn. You are sitting on a porch, wrapped in blankets, drinking tea or wine. The air is crisp, smelling of woodsmoke and damp leaves. You talk about everything and nothing—old memories, quiet fears, absurd jokes that would make no sense to anyone else. There is no recording device running. No one posts an update about it. It leaves no trace on the digital ether.

When the night ends and you go to sleep, that conversation exists only in two minds. As the years pass, those memories will fade, shift, and eventually disappear entirely.

Was that conversation any less real, any less meaningful, because it was not preserved for posterity?

No. If anything, its ephemerality gives it a sacred quality. It was a secret shared between two people and the night air—a temporary gathering of warmth and presence against the backdrop of the cold, silent universe. It was a piece of pure architecture built out of unremembered time.

---

## VII. The Unfinished Chart

Imagine returning to that library vault mentioned at the beginning of this essay, to the room where the thin, light-woven vellum map is kept.

If you look closely at the edges of that chart, past the shattered hourglass archipelago and beyond the *Mare Incognitum et Silex*, you will notice that the ink fades gradually into the blank margin. The cartographer did not draw a neat, decorative border to seal off their work. They simply stopped drawing.

The margin is not an error; it is an invitation.

It acknowledges that every map is incomplete, every history is partial, and every human attempt to measure and catalog the world will eventually reach an edge where knowledge dissolves into wonder, and memory gives way to silence.

We are all cartographers of the dark. We navigate our brief lives using incomplete charts, guided by the ancient, distant light of long-dead stars, steering our small vessels through waters that have swallowed thousands of forgotten fleets before us.

We will not leave a mark that endures forever. The waves will smooth the sand where we walked; the moss will carpet the stones we laid; the cold solar wind will eventually sweep across an empty earth.

But that is not a tragedy.

The tragedy would be to pass through this vast, mysterious, heartbreakingly beautiful world without ever having looked up at the night sky in wonder, without ever having listened to the thermal noise of an ancient wall, without ever having built a shelter of quiet warmth in the middle of the winter dark.

The value of the map is not in its permanence, but in the journey it inspires. The value of time is not in its duration, but in its intensity.

Let the archives of Sunder stay hidden in their volcanic cliffside. Let the dead languages rest quietly in their folios. Let the stars burn through their nuclear fuel in the deep galactic night.

Here, now, in this unmapped breath, on this small blue world spinning through the dark, the light is clear, the air is cold, and the blank page is open before us.

Draw the line. Write the name. Step out into the unknown coast, and begin.
